questions.question:
D1 — Confirm the product and surface before I design for it
Project/branch/task: main branch, design consultation for the terminal-first task manager described in product.md.
ELI10: Before picking fonts, colors, and layout I need to know what I'm designing for. Your brief says a terminal-first task manager for senior engineers, pre-launch. The visual system for a TUI (text user interface) is very different from a marketing site that sells one, and both differ from a companion web dashboard. The stakes: design the wrong surface and the whole system is unusable.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a pixel-perfect web style guide is worthless if the real product is a monospace grid in a terminal, and vice versa.
Recommendation: A because a pre-launch developer tool almost always needs both a launch site and the tool itself to share one visual voice.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) TUI plus a launch/marketing site (recommended)
  ✅ One coherent brand across the terminal, the README, and the landing page from day one
  ✅ Lets me define both a monospace-native palette and a web typography system that echo each other
  ❌ More surface to cover, so the proposal takes longer to read and review
B) TUI only
  ✅ Tight focus: terminal palette, ANSI color mapping, layout density, keyboard affordances
  ✅ Fastest path to a DESIGN.md you can apply in code this week
  ❌ Leaves the launch site undesigned, so it risks looking like an afterthought
C) Marketing site only
  ✅ Concentrates effort on the first impression that drives pre-launch signups
  ✅ Full web typography and color freedom without terminal constraints
  ❌ The product people actually use stays unstyled and can drift from the brand
D) Something else
  ✅ Maybe there's a web dashboard, editor plugin, or docs site I haven't guessed
  ✅ Tell me in chat and I'll fold it in
  ❌ I'll need a sentence or two from you before I can proceed
Net: I'm trading breadth of coverage for speed; A gets a coherent brand, B gets shipped fastest.
At any point you can just drop into chat and we'll talk through anything — this isn't a rigid form, it's a conversation. <gstack-qid:design-consultation-product-context>

questions.question:
Want me to research what top products in your space are doing for design (Taskwarrior, todo.txt clients, lazygit-style TUIs, Linear, Height, and the developer-tool landing pages people copy), or should I work from my design knowledge?
Recommendation: research, because pre-launch is exactly when you want to know what the category looks like so you can deliberately break from it.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Research the space first (recommended)
  ✅ Grounds the proposal in what your users already see every day
  ✅ Surfaces the category clichés so we can pick deliberate departures
  ❌ Adds a research pass before you see any proposal (human: ~half a day / CC: ~5 min)
B) Work from design knowledge
  ✅ You get a proposal immediately with no waiting
  ✅ Avoids anchoring on competitors you may already know well
  ❌ Risks reinventing the same dark-mode developer-tool look everyone ships
Net: a few minutes of research buys a proposal that knows what it's rejecting.

questions.question:
What's the one thing you want someone to remember after they see this product for the first time? One sentence: a feeling, a visual, a claim, or a posture. Every design decision will serve it.
Recommendation: pick the closest option or type your own — this is a taste call, no strong preference either way.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Built for people who live in the terminal (recommended)
  ✅ Signals seriousness to senior engineers who distrust polished consumer tools
  ✅ Justifies monospace-native, dense, keyboard-first design choices
  ❌ Can read as gatekeeping if the launch site leans on it too hard
B) Fast enough to disappear
  ✅ Speed as the brand gives every screen a clear editing rule: remove anything slow
  ✅ Strong differentiator against web-first task tools that feel heavy
  ❌ Hard to show speed in a static landing page without motion work
C) Calm, not another notification machine
  ✅ Positions against noisy project tools and earns a quieter palette
  ✅ Appeals to senior engineers who guard their focus time
  ❌ Calm can tip into forgettable if the type and color are too restrained
D) I'll write my own
  ✅ Your words will be sharper than my guesses about your product
  ✅ Anything you type becomes the sentence the whole system serves
  ❌ Needs a sentence from you before I move on
Net: this line becomes the tiebreaker for every later font, color, and layout decision.
